symbols.def: A kernel: a symmetric similarity function between two examples. Positive definite kernels are the ones this book studies.
The Gram matrix, the table of pairwise kernel values on a sample. Positive definiteness of the kernel means every Gram matrix is positive semidefinite.
The feature map sending an example into the feature space, with k(x,x') = \langle\Phi(x),\Phi(x')\rangle.
The reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) associated with a kernel: the space of functions in which the kernel acts as an inner product.
The RKHS inner product and norm. The norm measures smoothness: a small norm means a slowly varying function.
The representer of evaluation at x: the function whose RKHS inner product with any f returns f(x), the reproducing property.
The dual coefficients of a kernel machine. The representer theorem guarantees the solution has this finite form.
The regularization parameter weighting the RKHS-norm penalty against the data-fitting loss.
A loss function scoring the fit of a prediction. Different losses (squared, hinge, logistic, epsilon-insensitive) give different algorithms.
SVM slack variables and the trade-off parameters: C prices margin violations, and nu bounds the fraction of margin errors and support vectors.
The eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the kernel integral operator (Mercer's theorem). Their decay measures the smoothness the kernel enforces.
The kernel mean embedding of a probability distribution P into the RKHS.
The maximum mean discrepancy, the RKHS distance between the mean embeddings of P and Q.

terms.def: A symmetric function whose Gram matrix is positive semidefinite for every finite sample; equivalently, an inner product after a feature map.
A Hilbert space of functions in which evaluation is continuous and is carried out by an inner product with the kernel. Every positive definite kernel has a unique RKHS (Aronszajn).
Replacing every inner product in an algorithm by a kernel evaluation, so the algorithm runs in a feature space it never builds.
The minimizer of a regularized empirical risk over an RKHS lies in the span of the kernel functions at the training points, collapsing an infinite search to n coefficients.
Least-squares regression in an RKHS with a norm penalty; its solution is a linear system over the Gram matrix.
A margin-maximizing classifier: the hinge loss plus an RKHS penalty, whose solution depends only on the support vectors.
A training point with nonzero dual coefficient; the only points that determine an SVM's decision boundary.
A data-dependent capacity measure: how well a function class can correlate with random noise. Controls generalization for RKHS balls.
Principal component analysis run through the kernel: the eigendecomposition of the centered Gram matrix.
A continuous positive definite kernel on a compact domain expands as a uniformly convergent sum of its eigenfunctions, giving an explicit feature map.
A continuous translation-invariant kernel is the Fourier transform of a nonnegative measure; the basis of random Fourier features.
A kernel whose quadratic form is nonnegative on zero-sum coefficient vectors; k is CPD iff exp(tk) is positive definite for all t>0.
Haussler's framework building a kernel on structured objects by summing a kernel over all ways of decomposing them into parts; the umbrella over string, tree, and graph kernels.
A kernel whose mean embedding is injective, so MMD(P,Q)=0 only when P=Q; guaranteed by universality.
The RKHS distance between two distributions' mean embeddings, estimable from samples and used for two-sample testing.
A low-rank approximation of the Gram matrix from a subset of columns, one of the two main routes past the quadratic-memory wall.
A finite random feature map whose inner products approximate a translation-invariant kernel (via Bochner), reducing the kernel machine to a linear model.
Learning a convex combination of several kernels jointly with the predictor, a group-lasso over kernels.
The kernel governing an infinitely wide network's training in the lazy regime; one way deep networks connect to kernel machines.
The Gaussian process a randomly initialized infinite-width network converges to at its output, before any training; the network's function prior read as a kernel.

A distribution over functions in which any finite set of values is jointly Gaussian, specified by a mean and a covariance kernel; kernel ridge regression is its posterior mean with noise variance lambda·n.
A kernel whose RKHS is dense in the continuous functions on a compact domain, so it can approximate any target arbitrarily well; universality implies the kernel is characteristic.
The signed distance from a labeled point to a classifier's decision boundary; the SVM maximizes the smallest margin, and margin bounds control generalization.
The RKHS operator mapping the embedding of a conditioning variable to the mean embedding of a conditional distribution, extending mean embeddings to conditional laws.
A discrepancy between a sample and a target density that needs only the target's score function, built from a Stein operator acting on the RKHS; used for goodness-of-fit testing.

The generalization error curve that, past the interpolation threshold where a model fits the data exactly, descends a second time as capacity grows; the phenomenon that revised the classical bias-variance picture.
